response.title: how to get power to a shed without running electricity
response.answer:
You can get electricity to a shed without running electrical wiring from your house. The best solution depends on whether you need power for lights, tools, a computer, or something more demanding.

Here are four practical options.

1. Solar panels + battery (best for permanent power)
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop

Install solar panels on the shed roof and connect them to a battery system.

Cost: Approximately $500–$3,000+

Power: Lights, fans, laptops, security cameras, and some power tools

Pros: No connection to the house, quiet, renewable

Cons: Depends on sunlight and battery capacity

For example, a 400W solar array with a 2kWh battery could provide useful daily power for lights, electronics, and occasional small-tool use.

2. Portable power station (easiest solution)
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop

A portable power station is essentially a large rechargeable battery with standard electrical outlets.

Cost: Approximately $200–$1,500+

Power: LED lights, laptops, fans, small tools

Pros: No installation, plug-and-play, portable

Cons: Must recharge periodically

You can recharge it inside your house or add solar panels later.

This is probably the simplest option if you only use your shed occasionally.

3. Battery-powered lighting and tools (cheapest)
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop

If you only need lights and occasional tool use, you might not need traditional electrical outlets at all.

Cost: Approximately $30–$300

Power: LED lighting, cordless drills, fans

Pros: Very inexpensive, no electrical installation

Cons: Limited to battery-powered equipment

4. Portable generator (best for high-power tools)
Shop

A generator can power equipment that requires more electricity.

Cost: Approximately $400–$1,500+

Power: Saws, compressors, larger workshop equipment

Pros: High power output without permanent wiring

Cons: Noise, fuel costs, maintenance

Important: Fuel-powered generators must operate outdoors, well away from the shed, doors, windows, and vents because of carbon monoxide. Never run one inside the shed.
